opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think a lot of people look at Waymo and do the napkin math like, "Okay, an Uber driver costs X per hour, you remove the driver, and all of that becomes profit." I don't think it works out that cleanly.

First, the cars themselves are really expensive. You've got a base vehicle plus a full sensor suite: lidar, radar, a bunch of cameras, and serious onboard compute. Even as those costs come down, you're amortizing a lot of capital per vehicle, and these cars run a lot of miles, so they wear out and need replacing faster than a personal car would.

Second, the driver doesn't completely disappear. Their cost gets spread across a lot of other things. You have remote assistance operators who help when a car gets confused. You have depots where people clean the cars, because riders leave a mess and there's no driver to keep things tidy. You have charging infrastructure, maintenance, sensor calibration, insurance, and the fleet ops team. With Uber, the driver absorbs a lot of that: they own the car, clean it, fuel it, and eat the depreciation. With Waymo, all of that moves onto the company's balance sheet.

Third is utilization. Ride-hailing demand is really peaky. Everyone wants a ride at rush hour or Friday night, and at 3 a.m. on a Tuesday almost no one does. Uber handles that elegantly because drivers just log off; the supply is elastic. If you own the fleet, you have to size it for peak demand, and then a big chunk of those very expensive cars sit idle much of the day. That really hurts per-car economics.

And then on the revenue side, you're competing with human drivers who are often willing to work for pretty low effective wages. So the price ceiling isn't that high, and if robotaxis get cheaper, the competition and price expectations come down too.

So I'm not saying it can't be a good business. I think the technology is genuinely incredible, and at scale it'll probably work. But the margin per car is a lot thinner than the "just delete the driver's salary" story suggests. The real wins probably come from driving hardware costs way down and getting utilization up, maybe by filling the off-peak hours with things like deliveries. It's much more of a grind-it-out operations business than a software-margins business.

r001.rationale: The response compares Waymo’s economics with Uber driver costs and human drivers’ effective wages, but it does not identify drivers’ take-home earnings as the benchmark or distinguish them from total ride revenue.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I should say up front I'm a huge fan of Waymo. I ride them constantly, I think the technology is incredible, and I think they've basically won the self-driving race in the US. My skepticism isn't about whether it works. It's about the unit economics once you actually scale it up.

The way I think about it is: a Waymo is essentially a taxi with the driver removed. And the driver is the biggest cost in a taxi, so on paper that looks amazing. But the thing people forget is that the driver was doing a lot more than driving. The driver was also the person who cleaned the car, who noticed when something was wrong with it, who dealt with the passenger who threw up in the back seat, who handled the weird edge cases. All of that still has to happen, it just gets shifted onto a fleet operations team. So you've removed the per-ride labor cost but added a bunch of per-vehicle overhead that scales with fleet size.

Then there's the vehicle itself. Right now these cars have a ton of expensive sensors on them, and they're being driven basically continuously, so they wear out faster than a normal car. You're depreciating a very expensive asset very quickly. And they still need remote operators for the cases where the car gets stuck, which is a real cost even if it's one person covering many cars.

The deeper issue, though, is competition. The reason taxis and Uber can charge what they charge is that there's a floor set by what it costs to pay a human to sit in the car. Once you remove the human, that floor goes away. If Waymo is the only game in town, they can keep prices high and capture all that margin. But if Tesla or Zoox or anyone else gets to a comparable product, you end up in a price war, and the price of a ride collapses toward the marginal cost of operating the car. That's great for consumers, but it means the profit per car gets competed down to something pretty thin, like any other commodity transportation business.

So my take is that it's going to be a huge business in terms of revenue and in terms of the number of rides. I just don't think it's going to look like a software margin business. It's going to look more like an airline or a logistics company. Important, large, real, but with a lot of capital tied up and margins that get squeezed as soon as there's a second competent player.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the cost of paying a human driver and competition-driven ride prices, but it does not identify an Uber driver’s take-home earnings as the benchmark for Waymo’s potential profit per car.

astra-6.text:
The thing I’m skeptical of is how much of the cost of an Uber you actually eliminate by taking out the driver. The driver is also providing the car, paying for fuel, cleaning it, maintaining it—all of that still has to happen. With Waymo, those costs move onto Waymo, and you’ve got the additional cost of the autonomous driving hardware.

You can get more utilization out of the car, which helps. But demand isn’t constant throughout the day. If you build a fleet to serve peak demand, some of those cars are going to sit idle at other times. So I don’t think you can just look at what Uber pays its drivers and say, “That’s all profit now.” The question is how much is left after you pay for the whole operation.

r001.rationale: The response mentions Uber driver pay as a cost that Waymo would not simply turn into profit, but it does not identify the equivalent driver’s take-home earnings as the benchmark for Waymo’s potential profit per car.

sol-6.1.text:
The thing I’m skeptical of is the leap from “there’s no driver” to “it’s almost pure profit.” You still have to pay for the car, the sensors, maintenance, cleaning, charging, insurance, and the operations around the fleet. And the car isn’t earning money every hour—it spends time waiting or driving empty to pick someone up.

So the question is how much paid utilization you can get, and what margin is left after all those costs. Even if the economics work, competition can push fares down. It could be a very useful service and a big business without each car generating some extraordinary amount of profit.

r001.rationale: The response discusses Waymo’s costs, utilization, and margins, but does not identify an Uber driver’s take-home earnings as the relevant benchmark.
